c.tagline: Mexico's golden-age Pacific bay resort - cliff divers, beaches and nightlife - rebuilding after Hurricane Otis.

taxi.fareNote: Acapulco taxis are not metered and charge by zone - agree the fare before getting in. Uber and DiDi operate and are usually cheaper and safer, though taxi drivers sometimes restrict app pickups at the airport.

emergency.note: 911 is Mexico's unified emergency number for police, fire and ambulance; 078 is the national tourist assistance line.

avoid.reason: Stay out of non-tourist colonias such as Ciudad Renacimiento, Emiliano Zapata and Jardín, and the city's outskirts, where cartel-related violence is concentrated.
Stick to the Zona Dorada and Diamante hotel strips at night, avoid beaches after dark, and use hotel-arranged or app taxis.

hood_desc: The classic 'golden zone' along the Costera Miguel Aleman, lined with mid-century high-rise hotels, beach clubs, restaurants and Acapulco's famous nightlife, right on the main sweep of the bay; the busiest and most convenient base, though still recovering from Hurricane Otis.

Punta Diamante, the newer luxury zone southeast of the bay, with gated high-rise condos, big resorts, golf courses and the long Revolcadero surf beach; quieter and more polished than the Costera, but spread out and reliant on taxis.

Old Acapulco around the Zocalo, the Fort of San Diego and the small, calm Caleta and Caletilla beaches, plus the legendary La Quebrada cliff divers; the most historic, atmospheric and budget-friendly part of town.

A sheltered cove southeast of the main bay, known for its calm swimming, waterfront seafood palapas and a handful of upscale hotels tucked into the hills; a mellower, scenic alternative to the Costera.

A long, laid-back sandbar northwest of the city between the ocean and Coyuca Lagoon, famous for its dramatic Pacific sunsets, horseback riding and low-key beachfront guesthouses; the most relaxed, rustic stretch.

water.note: Drink bottled or purified water only, as locals do.

transit.hours: Buses and colectivos run roughly 05:00 to around 23:00 along the main Costera corridor, with far fewer after dark, when taxis or ride apps are the norm.
transit.note: Acapulco has no metro or rail; getting around means the cheap buses and colectivo vans along the Costera Miguel Aleman, taxis, or ride-hailing apps. Note the city is still rebuilding tourism infrastructure after Hurricane Otis struck in October 2023.
transit.pay: City buses and colectivo vans are paid in cash to the driver (roughly MXN 10-12 a ride); there is no rechargeable transit card. Many visitors ride the buses that run the length of the Costera between Old Acapulco and the Zona Dorada.

tip.r: ~10-15% at restaurants; round up for taxis and tip beach and hotel staff a few pesos.
